list.listitem: Most endocervical and endometrial polyps are asymptomatic.C
Endocervical polyps should be completely removed and submitted for histologic evaluation.C

Endometrial polyps can be visualized by transvaginal ultrasound as the first imaging modality of choice or hysterography; the latter has the highest diagnostic accuracy in infertile patients with suspected endometrial polyps.C The highest diagnostic accuracy for ultrasound is demonstrated with use of color-doppler, 3-D investigation and contrast.

The incidence of malignant change in an endocervical polyp is 0.2% to 0.4% and 0.5% to 3% among clinically-recognized endometrial polyps; further evaluation of the cervix and endometrium is recommended following detection.C All polyps should be sent for histopathological analysis.B
Consider endometrial evaluation in women older than 50 years with an identified cervical polyp or for women with a large cervical polyp.C
Patients on tamoxifen therapy with identified cervical polyps should undergo endometrial evaluation.C

Hysteroscopic polypectomy can be performed safely and effectively for pre- and post-menopausal women with abnormal vaginal bleeding if endometrial polyps are present.B Routine removal of polyps in sub-fertile women is not currently supported by evidence.

Removal of asymptomatic polyps in premenopausal women should be considered in patients with risk factors for endometrial cancer. In asymptomatic postmenopausal patients, polyps should be considered for removal if they are large (diameter >2 cm) or if they have risk factors for endometrial cancer.B

background.definition: Cervical polyps are hyperplastic proliferations of the cervix that are attached by a fibrovascular stalk and covered with varying proportions of columnar, squamous, or squamocolumnar epithelium. Cervical polyps more commonly originate from the endocervical canal and less frequently from the ectocervix.Endometrial polyps are localized intrauterine neoplasms composed of endometrial glands, stroma and blood vessels projecting from the uterine lining. They can be sessile or pedunculated and range in size from a few millimeters to several centimeters.

list.listitem: The reported prevalence of endocervical polyps in women undergoing routine gynecologic evaluation is 5%.

Reported prevalence rates for uterine/endometrial polyps in asymptomatic adult women range from 10% to 15% and are 20% to 30% in women with abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB). Another reviewer cited rates of endometrial polyps of 13%–50% in premenopausal women and 30% in postmenopausal women.

In a study of 686 Danish women (of 1660 invited), the prevalence of endometrial polyps was 7.8% (95% CI 5.6-9.9%) and increased with age. Polyps were rare among younger women (0.9% in those younger than 30 years). Most (82%) of the women with histopathologically-verified polyps were asymptomatic.
In a UK case series of 2625 women with postmenopausal bleeding, 387 (15%) had benign endometrial polyps and 34 (1.3%) had polyps containing hyperplasia or cancer.
Endometrial polyps were found in 9 of 81 patients using gender-affirming testosterone therapy who were undergoing hysterectomy.
Rates of endometrial polyps appear to be increased in women with infertility (6% to 32%). Polyps may alter endometrial receptivity and embryo implantation, reducing pregnancy rates.
Malignant change in an endocervical polyp is uncommon (0.2%-0.4%).Malignancy limited to the endocervical polyp (pedicle free of disease) is reported in 0.08%.
In a case series of 369 cervical polyps in women with a mean age of 46.5 years, 8 polyps (2.2%) showed squamous dysplasia and 6 (1.6%) had malignant or atypical and potentially malignant features.

The presence of a cervical polyp and 50 years of age or older are independent risk factors for the presence of an endometrial polyp. Malignant transformation is more common in endometrial polyps (0.5%-4.8%).
Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found rates of malignancy ranging from about 0.5% to 3% among clinically-recognized endometrial polyps.
A premalignant or malignant polyp occurs in 5.4% of postmenopausal women with endometrial polyps and 1.7% of reproductive-aged women with them, based on a systematic review of 17 studies.

In a UK case series of 2625 women with postmenopausal bleeding of whom 16% had an endometrial polyp, risk factors for hyperplasia and cancer in the polyp, occurring in 34 women, were endometrial thickness ≥10.8 mm (5.5-fold increased risk) and body mass index ≥32.5 kg/m2 (3.5-fold increased risk).

Authors of a systematic review of 37 studies of hysteroscopically-resected endometrial polyps found the following risk factors associated with malignant lesions within the polyp: age >60 years (prevalence ratio [PR] 2.41, 95% CI, 1.84-3.16), diabetes mellitus (PR 1.76, 95% CI, 1.43-2.16), menopausal status (PR 1.67, 95% CI, 1.48-1.89; I2), tamoxifen use (PR 1.53, 95% CI 1.06-2.21), systemic arterial hypertension (PR 1.50, 95% CI, 1.20-1.88), abnormal uterine bleeding (PR 1.47, 95% CI, 1.27-1.69), and obesity (PR 1.41; 95% CI, 1.13-1.76).

In an Italian study including 1404 patients with endometrial polyps of whom 2.2% were diagnosed as either atypical hyperplasia or cancer, prevalence was increased among those who were overweight, over age 54 years, or with a polyp over 2 cm in size.

In one study, a combination of the presence of abnormal uterine bleeding (82.2% vs. 35.1% for those with benign lesions), large polyps (dimension 1.91 ± 1.00 cm vs. 1.34 ± 0.71 cm, respectively) and the ratio of blood flow signal detected on preoperative transvaginal ultrasound (64.3% vs. 35.2%, respectively) were useful in predicting malignancy with an area under the ROC curve of 0.80, sensitivity of 91% and negative predictive value of 96%.
Lobular breast cancer was reported to spread to an endometrial polyp in one case report.
The coexistence of endometrial polyps in women with uterine fibroids was 20.1% in a study of 772 women who underwent hysterectomy because of uterine fibroids.

Pre-menopausal women with endometrial polyps had an increased prevalence of chronic endometritis (51%) compared to women without endometrial polyps (OR 3.1, 95% CI 1.6-5.9``) based on a meta-analysis of 8 observational studies. Similarly, among infertile women in one retrospective study, the prevalence of chronic endometritis was significantly higher in women with endometrial polyps than women without polyps (45.3% vs. 27.9%). However, authors using large scale genetic data did not find evidence suggesting that the presence of endometritis was associated with a higher endometrial polyp risk.

There was an increased prevalence of colorectal polyps among postmenopausal patients with endometrial polyps compared to patients without endometrial polyps in one study (18 of 57 [31.6%] vs. 6 of 71 [8.4%]).
In an Australian study, metabolic syndrome was present in 32 (71.1%) of 45 women with endometrial polyps compared to 6 (13.3%) of 45 women without endometrial polyps.
The etiology of endocervical polyps is unclear.
Polyps may occur as a response to local inflammation, chronic irritation, localized vascular congestion, or an abnormal focal response to hormonal stimulation.

While the cause of endometrial polyps is also unknown, growth is linked to estrogen stimulation which may result from increased concentration of estrogen receptors, difference in dominant type of receptor (e.g., predominantly estrogen receptor-alpha in polyp glandular cells compared with normal endometrium), and/or a decreased expression of progesterone receptors in polyps.
Localized inflammation may also play a role as elevated levels of cyclooxygenase-2 and mast cells are found in endometrial polyps.
Polyp formation occurs as a result of focal hyperplasia of the epithelium; the pathogenesis in unknown.

Ectocervical polyps are covered by stratified squamous epithelium and endocervical polyps are covered by squamocolumnar or metaplastic squamous epithelium. Most cervical polyps arise from the endocervix. Endometrial polyps often contain a parallel arrangement of the endometrial glands' long axis to the surface epithelium.
Endocervical polyps are histologically divided into six categories: adenomatous, cystic, fibrous, vascular, fibromyxomatous, and inflammatory.
The majority of endocervical polyps are adenomatous.
Stromal cell chromosomal abnormalities may have a role in the development of endometrial polyps.

It is likely that both estrogen-related and non-estrogen-related pathways lead to endometrial polyp formation. Risk factors include aging, obesity, long-term tamoxifen use (9% in one study), and unbalanced estrogen therapy; protective factors include progestin use. Among conditions causing hyperestrogenism, obesity, polycystic ovary syndrome, late menopause, estrogen-secreting gonadal stromal tumors and chronic liver disease are the most frequently associated with endometrial polyp formation.

Differences are found between normal endometrium and endometrial polyp tissue. For example, there are higher levels of transforming growth factor beta-1, associated with fibrotic tissue formation, and vascular endothelial growth factor, an angiogenic factor, in endometrial polyps.
Combined estrogen-progesterone oral contraceptives or continuous progesterone therapy may have a protective effect on the incidence of cervical polyps.

Administration of progesterone may increase regression rates of endometrial polyps. In one study, women given 25 mg subcutaneous progesterone during the luteal phase for 7 days for 3 months had a regression rate of endometrial polyps of 47.5% vs. 12.5% for women who refused progesterone treatment. This author was unable to identify any RCTs supporting this treatment.

In a case series of 397 postmenopausal women at increased risk of endometrial polyp recurrence, endometrial resection or ablation reduced recurrence rates to 5% overall at 60 months, but was higher among women on tamoxifen (13%). Most women (90%) had no complications but 8 women (2%) suffered intraoperative cervical lacerations; 8 had uterine perforation, treated conservatively; 8 suffered fluid overload without electrolyte disturbances, 1 developed infection, 1 had a uterine hemorrhage and 12 women had post-puncture headache.

Similarly, in a single-blind clinical trial including 94 women with endometrial polyps, those randomized to hysteroscopic polypectomy plus endometrial resection had fewer polyp recurrences compared with those randomized to hysteroscopic polypectomy alone (two [4.3%] and nine [19.1%], respectively).
Endocervical polyps can be visualized on speculum examination or colposcopy.C

Transvaginal ultrasonography is the imaging modality of choice for detection of endometrial polyps in woman of fertile age.C However, in-office hysteroscopy has the highest diagnostic accuracy in infertile patients with suspected endometrial polyps.C
Endocervical polyps should be completely removed under colposcopic guidance and submitted for histologic evaluation.C
Ambulatory polypectomy under colposcopy is well tolerated if the polyp pedicle is visible under forceps traction, with minimal to no complications.B
Broad-based polyps should be removed under anesthesia or during hysteroscopy because of bleeding risk.C
Endometrial polyps can be diagnosed and safely and effectively removed with hysteroscopy.B

list.listitem: Most endocervical polyps (60%-75%) are asymptomatic incidental findings discovered during routine screening. Most endocervical polyps occur in the late reproductive and perimenopausal years; 90% occur at 40 years or older, 45% to 64% occur in postmenopausal women, and 75% occur in multiparous women.

Endocervical polyps can cause postcoital or postmenopausal bleeding, intermenstrual spotting, irregular bleeding, heavy menstrual bleeding, or leukorrhea. The most common reported symptom is excessive bleeding at or between mentrual cycles followed by postmenopausal bleeding.
Abnormal uterine bleeding`` is common with endometrial polyps, occurring in approximately 68% of both pre- and postmenopausal women.

Endocervical polyps can be visualized on speculum examination or colposcopy. They are smooth, soft, glistening, often tear-shaped pedunculated lesions that appear reddish-purple to cherry red, and project through the cervical os. They are vascular and friable, can be single (88%-90%) or multiple in number, and can range in size up to several centimeters but usually measure less than 3 cm (86% measure 1 cm or less).

Endometrial polyps appear as projections from the uterine lining and range in size from about 5 mm to filling the uterine cavity; most are located in the uterine fundus. While endometrial polyps can be found in all age groups, they are most commonly diagnosed in patients between the ages 40 and 49 years. Polyps that have irregular surfaces, are ulcerative, and have vascular abundance during hysteroscopy are more suspicious for malignancy.

Potential biomarkers are under investigation for determining benign from malignant endometrial polyps. In one study, a panel of serum lipidomics (lipid metabolites) yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.915, sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 72% for distinguishing endometrial polyps from endometrial cancer.

Colposcopy is often performed to assess cervical lesions; however, cervical cytology and colposcopy alone are insufficient for evaluating an endocervical polyp. Colposcopic diagnostic accuracy alone is 56.3% and increases to 75% when combined with cytology.

In addition to cervical cytology and colposcopy, diagnosis requires polypectomy and histologic evaluation. Ambulatory polypectomy under colposcopy is well tolerated if the pedicle root is visualized under forceps traction.

Hysteroscopic polypectomy and/or polypectomy under anesthesia is recommended if the base of the pedicle is not visualized or if the polyp is broad based. Outpatient hysteroscopy provides direct visualization of the polyp, direct visualization to address hemostasis, and an opportunity to identify and treat concurrent intrauterine pathology.
Gel sonovaginography, in which 20 mL of ultrasound gel is instilled into the vagina followed by examination with a transvaginal transducer, may be useful in visualizing cervical polyps.

Transvaginal ultrasonography is the imaging modality of choice for detection of endometrial polyps in woman of fertile age. Accuracy of ultrasound increases with use of color-doppler, 3-D investigation and contrast.

However, in a Portuguese prospective observational study with 307 patients comparing transvaginal ultrasound performed at various centers to hysteroscopy as the reference standard, sensitivity was 40% and specificity was 73% for endometrial polyps. These investigators recommended hysteroscopy.

In a small study comparing the test characteristics of intrauterine ultrasound and hysteroscopy for endometrial polyps using surgical and pathological examination methods as the gold standard, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of ultrasonography in the diagnosis of endometrial polyps were 90.0%, 66.7%, and 87.9%, respectively; those of hysteroscopy were 96.7%, 66.7%, and 93.9%, respectively; and combined diagnosis was 96.7%, 100.0%, 97.0%, 100.0%, and 75.0%.

Three-dimensional transvaginal ultrasound, as noted above, had better performance characteristics based on a retrospective study of 500 women aged 19 to 46 years with uterine lesions. In this study, sensitivity of ultrasound was 95% and specificity 97% for endometrial polyp detection.

Polyp size is a consideration, as one group of investigators found a positive predictive value for TVUS, based on 295 patients referred for hysteroscopy, of 79% overall and 92% for those with endometrial polyps ≥1.5 cm.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommend transvaginal ultrasonography as usually sufficient for initial evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding if the ultrasound images reveal an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less, which has a >99% negative predictive value for endometrial cancer.

In one study of 200 women in the Netherlands with postmenopausal bleeding, an endometrial thickness >4 mm and a benign result from endometrial sampling, there was no difference in recurrent bleeding at 1 year between those randomized to hysteroscopy and those randomized to expectant management (15.3% vs. 18%, respectively). However, in the hysteroscopy group, 50/98 (51%) were found to have endometrial polyps of which 6 showed evidence of premalignancy or malignancy; three with hyperplasia with atypia and 3 with endometrial cancer on final pathology.

Authors of an evidence-based review recommend against use of dilation and curettage for diagnosis and management of polyps as it prevents diagnosis of focal uterine pathology. They recommend that all polyps be sent for histopathological analysis

Sonohysterography may be reasonable as a first-line test for premenopausal women with AUB. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 studies comparing two-dimensional saline contrast sonohysterography to standard hysteroscopy for detection of endometrial polyps in women of reproductive age with AUB found a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 93% (95% CI, 89-96%) and 81% (95% CI, 76-86%), respectively, with pooled LR+ of 5.41 (95% CI, 2.60-11.28) and LR- of 0.10 (95% CI, 0.06-0.17).

Based on an evidence-based review, postmenopausal women with vaginal bleeding and suspected endometrial polyp should be offered diagnostic hysteroscopy with hysteroscopic polypectomy if endometrial polyps are present.

list.listitem: In a retrospective study of 53 female patients (37 cases with endometrial carcinoma and 16 cases with endometrial polyps confirmed by surgical resection or biopsy), magnetic resonance imaging using combination amide proton transfer weighted imaging with intra-voxel incoherent motion imaging improved diagnostic accuracy.

In a retrospective observational study analysis including 365 patients with endometrial polyps who underwent saline infusion sonohysterography, mean polyp size was 17.7 ± 0.5 mm in patients with benign disease compared to 23.7 ± 1.8 mm in those with premalignant/malignant polyps.
Most cervical polyps are benign asymptomatic incidental findings; symptoms can include postmenopausal bleeding, intermenstrual spotting, irregular bleeding, heavy menstrual bleeding, or leukorrhea.
Cervical polyps can be visualized on speculum examination or colposcopy but diagnosis requires polypectomy and histologic evaluation.
Cervical polyps are removed more often because of their tendency to cause abnormal bleeding than for their risk of malignancy (0.2%-0.4%), thereby eliminating a potential source for bleeding.
Consider endometrial evaluation for women 50 years or older and for women identified with a large cervical polyp or in women taking tamoxifen.

Premenopausal women with AUB and postmenopausal women with vaginal bleeding and suspected endometrial polyp should be offered diagnostic hysteroscopy with hysteroscopic polypectomy if endometrial polyps are present.

There is general consensus that cervical polyps should be removed to prevent potential future abnormal vaginal bleeding, to assess for malignancy, and because the risk of outpatient removal is minimal. However, caution is advised with removal during pregnancy.C
Consider endometrial evaluation for women 50 years or older and for women identified with a cervical polyp while taking tamoxifen.C

Although many experts favor hysteroscopy, which provides direct visualization of the polyp peduncle and the opportunity to identify and treat concurrent intrauterine pathology, there are insufficient data to recommend one endometrial sampling modality over another.C
When malignant change is identified in an endocervical polyp, further evaluation should be performed to look for associated cervical and/or endometrial abnormalities.C

Hysteroscopic polypectomy can be performed safely and effectively for pre- and post-menopausal women with abnormal vaginal bleeding if endometrial polyps are present.B Polypectomy does not appear to compromise reproductive outcomes. Despite an association between endometrial polyps and infertility and subfertility, routine removal of polyps in sub-fertile women is not currently supported by evidence.B

Removal of asymptomatic polyps in premenopausal women should be considered in patients with risk factors for endometrial cancer. In asymptomatic postmenopausal patients, polyps should be considered for removal if they are large (diameter >2 cm) or of they have risk factors for endometrial cancer.B

Most endocervical polyps can be removed in an outpatient setting with the assistance of a clamp/forceps under colposcopic guidance. The base of the polyp is firmly grasped with forceps and avulsed with a gentle twisting motion and/or the pedicle is excised with scissors. Cautery may be required to destroy the base and ensure hemostasis.
Broad-based polyps should be removed under anesthesia or hysteroscopy because of bleeding risk.
Hysteroscopic polypectomy can be performed safely and effectively for pre- and post-menopausal women with abnormal vaginal bleeding if endometrial polyps are present.

In a case series of 397 postmenopausal women undergoing endometrial resection or ablation, most (90%) women had no complications, eight (2%) suffered intraoperative cervical lacerations; 8 had uterine perforation, treated conservatively; 8 suffered fluid overload without electrolyte disturbances, 1 developed infection, 1 uterine hemorrhage and 12 women had post-puncture headache.

Removal of asymptomatic polyps in premenopausal women should be considered in patients with risk factors for endometrial cancer; in asymptomatic postmenopausal patients, polyps should be considered for removal if they are large (diameter >2 cm) or of they have risk factors for endometrial cancer. Risk factors for malignancy are listed in the section on other impact above.
If atypical hyperplasia or carcinoma is identified on a polyp, hysterectomy is recommended in all post-menopausal patients and in premenopausal patients without desire of future fertility.

Based on a retrospective study including 166 patients, the 64 patients undergoing hysteroscopic polypectomy with a rigid scope reported less pain than the 102 patients who underwent a polypectomy with a semirigid hysteroscope.

In a randomized controlled non-inferiority trial including 66 women with symptomatic endometrial polyps, use of a a tissue removal device vs. an electrosurgical polyp snare resulted in a higher rate of complete polyp resection (95% vs. 57%), overall safety and higher patient satisfaction.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 studies including 334 patients with endometrial polyps concluded that hysteroscopic 2 μm laser vaporesection was superior to hysteroscopic electroresection with respect to blood loss, length of hospital stay, recurrence and complication rates.

Successful hysteroscopic endometrial polyp removal was also reported using bipolar loop hysteroscope without electricity in a case series including 25 women; no cases of bleeding or complications were reported.

Based on long-term follow up of 55 women (71% of the original randomization cohort) who underwent hysteroscopic endometrial polypectomy, there were no statistically significant differences in recurrence or persistence of abnormal uterine bleeding between a manually and motor driven hysteroscopic tissue removal system for polypectomy. Mean time to recurrence or persistence of abnormal uterine bleeding was 26 months and 29 months, respectively.

Expectant management can be considered, especially for younger, asymptomatic women with endometrial polyps. Authors of a retrospective cohort study followed 1006 women with asymptomatic endometrial polyps managed expectantly (55.5%) or with hormonal drugs (44.5%). Over a mean observation time of 14.1 ± 18.5 months, the overall regression rate of polyps was 8.9% after expectant management and 24.6% after medication. Patient age (<50 years), follow-up period, and hormonal drugs used were significantly associated with regression. Twenty-four (7.1%) of the 337 patients who experienced regression later developed recurrent disease.

Consider endometrial sampling in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women 50 years or older. Women using tamoxifen therapy with an identified cervical polyp should undergo polyp removal and endometrial evaluation to rule out concomitant endometrial pathology, particularly endometrial carcinoma.C

Authors of a retrospective study of 221 women (128 postmenopausal) with asymptomatic cervical polyps found that polyp size >19 mm and volume >2300 mm was associated with premalignant or malignant endometrial lesions; the 1 lesion showing hyperplasia with atypia and the 3 malignancies occurred among postmenopausal women. They recommend endometrial sampling in these cases.

Blind (without direct visualization) Pipelle sampling provides more accurate endometrial sampling if the pathology is global rather than focal. Focal endometrial lesions, such as polyps, can be missed.

Blind dilatation and curretage (D&C) provides endometrial sampling but may miss up to 17% of lesions found during hysteroscopy. D&C does not allow for selected tissue sampling and has less sensitivity than hysteroscopy. Pedunculated polyps, in particular, may be too mobile to be detected, and sessile polyps may be torn into unrecognizable fragments.
Hysteroscopy provides direct visualization of the intrauterine cavity and can identify focal lesions.
When malignant change is identified in an endocervical polyp, further evaluation should be performed to look for associated cervical and/or endometrial abnormalities.
Up to one quarter of endometrial polyps regress spontaneously.

In a retrospective follow-up study in the UK of 112 women with endometrial polyps who were not on hormone therapy and were managed expectantly, annual endometrial polyp growth rate varied, with a median of 1.0% (interquartile range, -6.5 to 14.3). Seven of the 112 women had complete polyp regression over a median follow-up period of 28 months; regression was more frequent in premenopausal women. Eleven out of 75 women who initially did not have AUB subsequently developed abnormal bleeding. Polyp growth rate was not associated with the subsequent development of AUB

Among 197 women who underwent operative hysteroscopy but preferred follow-up for identified endometrial polyps, 10 of 74 (13.5%) who returned for operative hysteroscopy within one month did not have polyps identified and 28 of 123 (23%) who returned between 30 and 360 days after the initial procedure no longer had polyps visualized. Patients who were <45 years, premenopausal, with small polyp size (<2 cm), and AUB were more likely to have no polyps found on reinvestigation

The recurrence rate following outpatient cervical polypectomy is approximately 2%.B However, higher recurrence rates have been reported of between 7.7% for women on tamoxifen for breast cancer, and 15% when using a grasping forceps for removal.

Recurrence of benign endometrial polyps after hysteroscopic polypectomy based on long-term follow-up (9 years), is similar at about 3%. Recurrence rate is higher (up to 10%), however, in cases with multiple polyps and hyperplastic polyps.

Much higher recurrence rates were reported in a Chinese case series of 133 patients undergoing initial hysteroscopic polypectomy. Of 124 women who underwent at least 12 months of follow-up with ultrasound examination every 3 months, 98 (79%) had a recurrence. Risk factors for recurrence based on logistic regression were age, body mass index, polyp size and endometrial thickness; progesterone therapy after first polypectomy was a protective factor.

The presence of cervical polyps in early pregnancy appears to be a risk factor for late abortion and spontaneous preterm delivery. In a retrospective cohort study of 2941 singleton pregnant women in whom 142 (4.8%) had cervical polyps with removal performed in 25.4%, cervical polyp was an independent risk factor for late abortion (OR 13.0, 95% CI 3.3–51.4) and spontaneous preterm birth before 28-weeks gestation (OR 4.6, 95% CI 1.1–18.6). Although many of the cervical polyps regressed during pregnancy, regression did not reduce the risk of preterm birth or cervical insufficiency.

In a retrospective cohort study including 4172 pregnant patients who visited a tertiary perinatal center before 12 weeks of gestation, 92 (2.2%) had a cervical polyp detected before 12 weeks of gestation and treated expectantly. The incidence of spontaneous preterm birth before 34 weeks of gestation was higher in those with cervical polyps (5.4% vs 0.7% in those without them).
In a case series of 3 pregnant patients, ultrasound was useful in determining the origin of cervical polyps allowing for successful polypectomy.

In one case series of removal of cervical polyps during the first or second trimester of pregnancy, the pathological diagnosis was 41 decidual polyps and 42 endocervical polyps. Women with decidual polypectomy had a higher risk of spontaneous abortion (12.2% vs. 0%) and preterm delivery (34.2% vs. 4.8%) than women following removal of an endocervical polyp. The authors recommend waiting until delivery to consider removal of what appears to be a cervical polyp.

In a more recent case series of 307 pregnant patients who underwent cervical polypectomy, 8.8% had a miscarriage before 28 weeks and 12.1% had a preterm delivery. The presence of decidual polyps and vaginal bleeding after polypectomy were the risk factors for miscarriage; 14.9% of patients with decidual polyps miscarried compared to 5.6% of those with endocervical polyps.
Hysteroscopic polypectomy has been shown to increases chances for successful pregnancy after intrauterine insemination.
